Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a post about why a company is investing in developer relations. Around 250 words.

Why we're hiring for developer relations

We shipped an SDK in March and watched the support queue tell us what the docs didn't. Roughly a third of the tickets were people who had installed correctly and then guessed wrong about what to do next, because the quickstart ended before the part they actually needed. Our engineers answered those tickets. They answered them well, and slowly, between other work.

That's the gap we're funding. Developer relations here means someone whose full-time job is the space between the API existing and someone using it successfully: rewriting the getting-started path, sitting in the Discord, building the sample apps we keep promising, and carrying what they hear back into the roadmap instead of into a slide.

We're deliberately not framing this as marketing. The role reports into engineering, and the first six months have no talk quota. The measure is whether time-to-first-successful-call drops from the current median of 47 minutes, and whether the support queue stops absorbing questions that a better tutorial would have answered.

There's a version of this job that goes badly, where the person becomes a conference travel budget with a Twitter account and no influence on the product. We've seen it. The protection is that they'll have commit access to the docs repo and a standing slot in sprint planning, so the feedback loop is short enough to matter.

We're a company whose product is an interface other engineers have to learn. Someone should own how that learning goes. Right now nobody does, and the cost of that shows up in the queue every week.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

Return only the rewritten text.

Why we're hiring for developer relations

We shipped an SDK in March and watched the support queue tell us what the docs didn't. Roughly a third of the tickets were people who had installed correctly and then guessed wrong about what to do next, because the quickstart ended before the part they actually needed. Our engineers answered those tickets. They answered them well, and slowly, between other work.

That's the gap we're funding. Developer relations here means someone whose full-time job is the space between the API existing and someone using it successfully: rewriting the getting-started path, sitting in the Discord, building the sample apps we keep promising, and carrying what they hear back into the roadmap instead of into a slide. The role is one person, not a team, and it starts in October.

We're deliberately not framing this as marketing. The role reports into engineering, and the first six months have no talk quota. The measure is whether time-to-first-successful-call drops from the current median of 47 minutes, and whether the support queue stops absorbing questions that a better tutorial would have answered. Those are the two numbers we'll look at in April, and if neither moves we'll have learned something about our own assumptions rather than about the hire.

There's a version of this job that goes badly, where the person becomes a conference travel budget with a Twitter account and no influence on the product. We've seen it. The protection is that they'll have commit access to the docs repo and a standing slot in sprint planning.

Our product is an interface other engineers have to learn. Someone should own how that learning goes. Right now nobody does, and the cost shows up in the queue every week.
